utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. May I remind you, Mr. Berghofer, of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence which still supplies. We will now continue with your evidence. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just as yesterday, please make a small pause after my questions so that the interpreters may have sufficient time to interpret everything we're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would also like to have the usher's assistance, please, to give the witness a set of statements that the Defence will be cross-examining on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, I would like to go back briefly to what you talked about yesterday about those things that were happening in the hangar. Do you remember if anybody described the people who were inside the hangar while you were there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, nobody asked and nobody wrote letters, as people say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about anybody taking down the names of the people from your group on your way out of the hangar, those from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did anybody take your names down, the group of five or six people who you said were taken out of the hangar and returned to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I remember, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If I were to tell you that we have heard witnesses who claim that names were taken down in the hangar, especially in relation to your group, the group that went back to Vukovar, would you still stick to your previous statement and say that there was no such thing or maybe you just didn't see it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the two hours I was inside the hangar, nobody drew up any lists or took any names down. There may be someone else who remembers better than I do, and well done in that case. I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, I'm about to move on to a different topic now. It's in relation to that list of people you saw at Ovcara which you gave to my learned friend here and which has been tendered into evidence as Exhibit 228. Mr. Berghofer, you said that upon your return to Croatia in March 1992, you compiled a list comprising 23 persons that you then believed to have seen at Ovcara. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Vasic. As many as 25, perhaps. Between 22 and 25 I'd say. These were just names that I remember because there was no way to forget them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you in fact use these lists when you spoke to people from the Croatian authorities, from the Ministry of the Interior when you gave your statements and they compiled official notes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, our people back in Croatia had no idea who had been at Ovcara until I came along, and I was the first to give them about 25 or 27 different names. I was the first to identify those people simply because most of those people were neighbours. We lived in the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did I get this right? Does this mean that you were in touch with the Croatian government, commission for missing persons, and did you give these lists to them, too?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I've lost track about how many times I gave those statements about all the missing persons, so they were probably one of the recipients. For example, in Belgrade, Vesko Krstajic, the judge, gave me a complete list and asked me to circle whichever names seemed familiar, which means that there were even more people on various lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Before you testified in Belgrade in 2004, did you have occasion to speak to the missing persons commission and go through that list of people who were claimed to have gone missing at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Vasic. It's been 14 years after all. If I confirm while unsure and if I deny with no certainty in sight, there's no point in -- to the whole exercise at all. Mr. Vasic, there's no need for anybody to wave lists from Ovcara in front of my face. You have Pero Simic, for example, who was only a hundred metres away from me and I didn't take his name down. There were people I still remembered at the time, but by the time I got down to it I could no longer remember their names. It is you who make me think back to all these things that happened at Ovcara and old images begin to flick through my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: There's something I need to ask you, Mr. Berghofer. You've spent the last 15 years, on and off at least, talking to the various bodies of the Croatian authorities testifying in front of tribunals. Is it that throughout all this time you were not really able to clearly remember all the names at any point, the same situation as you claim to be in now, in other words?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That sounds about right, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This list that you've been shown by my learned friends which is attached to the indictment, it was shown to you before your testimony with the list of persons who allegedly went missing at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't like that, Mr. Vasic. I had to compile a list of my own just like that, off the bat.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the list that you drew up in March 1992? You used that one, didn't you, in your interviews with the different bodies that you spoke to. You also used this list during your testimony before the chamber of the special court and Judge Vesko Krstajic at the Belgrade trial?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I relied on my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What I want to know is: Do you keep that list in your house, did you leave it behind, or do you have it on you here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the list on me, Mr. Vasic. I haven't touched that list for eight years. It's just a small slip of paper from one of my folders. It was the last sheet in the folder, and I just jotted a couple of things down. It was the same day that I was released, and I have not touched it since. I haven't added anything to it since or taken any of the names away from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you use this list while giving your statement to the officials of the Ministry of the Interior on the 6th of April, 1992? It's a statement of yours that we discussed yesterday, you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I probably used the list. I probably used the list. You can start out with that assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when it was that you in fact remembered these nine new persons who weren't originally on your list? Was that after Belgrade, after your testimony before the Belgrade court, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're quite right, Mr. Vasic. Some before and some after Belgrade. And sometimes I just bumped into one of their relatives. I was just getting confused about some surnames yesterday, and it was at the last minute that I finally remembered. Therefore, I don't keep all the 30 or 40 names in my head at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Throughout the last 15 years, did you speak to Mr. Cakalic or to anybody else who knew anything about Ovcara about these events?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, to be perfectly frank, Cakalic lives far away from me, 700 or 800 kilometres; he lives somewhere on the coast now. I met Guncevic before I first went to The Hague in 1995, 1996. He lived in Zagreb at the time. He probably still does. I met Mladen Karlovic back in 1996 when we arrived here. I met Zarko Kojic in 1996, likewise. I didn't even recognise him at first. He had grown so, so much. I saw him before our departure for Belgrade. I also met Cakalic, I'm not sure about the year, it was the same year that five of your colleagues from Belgrade came over to Zagreb and we gave a statement. We just exchanged greetings. He was on his way out, and we shook hands. Then he left. As for the statements, I did tell you that these lads were my neighbours for the most part or my friends' children.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Berghofer. I just have two related questions. You said they were either neighbours on your friends' children, but they still weren't on your original list. Some of the names you only remember later on, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you meet Mr. Cakalic before your testimony before the chamber of the special crimes court in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First they came to get me and then we drove to Borovo, I think he was staying with his daughter at the time, and then after that we were off to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You arrived in Belgrade together, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you talk on your way there about your testimony, about your memories?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we really discussed most of the time was how each of us got by in this new country that we now had, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Something else I need to ask you about these testimonies. Were you part of that commission in 1992, the one that met in Budapest to give certain statements to some representatives of the international community, Yugoslavia, and Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Vasic. I wasn't one of the people who made up that delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Exhibit 228 placed on the screen; that's the list. I don't have this on my screen. I do have a hard copy, though, which I can hand to the witness. I will go -- I hope we now have it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, you have it on the screen now, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me this, please, I'll take one name at a time and you tell me if you know whether any of these people were members of the National Guards Corps or Vukovar's defenders. Can you do that for me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Mr. Vasic, but I'd like to help you first with this, so if you just hear me out. I'll read the names out for you of people whose names were first taken down back in 1992, and then I can mark out for you the names that I remember later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gavric, Dragan; Veber, Sinisa.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just a little more slowly so all the names may be accurately recorded.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlaho, he was an ambulance driver with the hospital. I don't know his name, but he was one of my neighbours, too. Goran Vidos. His father was my boss. Pavlovic, Zeljko I think was his first name. He lived just across the way from me. Sinisa Glavasevic, I made no special notes. Everybody knew he was a journalist. Lili I couldn't remember at first. He was a young lad, and I didn't remember him at first. Number 8 is Jurela. I didn't know his first name, so I just wrote down Tomo Jurela's son, and his mother's Zlatka, she's a nurse. Zvonko Iles, we used to call him Zriko when we were children. We grew up together. Branko Polomija. I just couldn't for the life of me remember anything about him at the time, but I know that he worked for Radio Vukovar. Number 11 and number 12, the Kolak brothers. I used to work with their father. For a long time we worked in the same company. And the young lads lived above my shop in Patkoviceva Street. It's all nearby. Stjepan Herman, I've pointed that out already. That is Stjepan Sarac's [phoen] who manned the phones and he lived above the shop. Svabo, last name Herman, likewise, but his grand-dad or grand-grand-dad grand-grand-grand-dad left Yugoslavia in 1962 or 1963, perhaps even earlier, I really don't know. And the old Herman, the driver, the haulier, the bus driver, he said himself when he came, he came in uniform. He was armed. And we asked him: Well, which one are you? And he said: I'm Herman nicknamed Svabo. Ante Bodruzic was one of the bosses at the Danube hotel, head waiter or something. I did some upholstery work for him. He was a client of mine and that's the reason I remember him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, can you slow down a little so that all the names can be recorded.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, I agree. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Bodruzic, was he on the original list?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was no way I could have forgotten about him. Ivo Kovac who was Mate Kovac's son. We used to work together for years. He worked at the post office until the very last day. Dragica Tuskan, she must have been born in 1963, 1964, 1965, and we were neighbours in the Katic Street, and after 1970 we started working together at the Stjepan Supanc Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, I do apologise. You've already provided us with the information about these people in answer to the OTP. Just so as not to repeat everything, can you just tell me who was on the original list and who wasn't, so as not to waste any time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, that's what I'm telling you at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just admit one small thing, because I'm well aware of the difficulties that can develop with this list having dealt with it. For my part, it's often easier if one deals with the actual number of the individual and for the question to be asked, Was he on the original list or was he not. And if it's done systematically that way, I suspect we'll get clearer answers, otherwise it will be very difficult to find exactly what is what. I know it's slightly mundane, but I for my part have found that to be the best part of dealing with the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Vasic will be grateful. Could we just confirm, Mr. Berghofer, the names so far on the list, were they all on your original list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Vasic, we may need to go back to the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, unfortunately, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Berghofer, in order to be even more expedient, we can do it in the following way. I'll give you the numbers and the names and you will then tell me whether that person was on the original list, yes or no. Can you do it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a correction, Mr. Vasic, what list do you have in mind? It is not clear to me, what first list? Which one is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That's the list you compiled in March 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I do understand. Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So number 1 on the list you compiled here in The Hague, Dragan Gavric, was he on the original list?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 2, Sinisa Veber?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 3, a person called Vlaho?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 4, Goran Vidos?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 5, Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 6, Sinisa Glavasevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 7, a person called Lili?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 8, a person called Jurela?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 9, Zvonko Iles?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 10, Branko Polomija?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 11, Kolak; and number 12, Kolak as well, the Kolak brothers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 13, Stjepan Herman, is that it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 14, Herman called Svabo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 15, Ante Bodruzic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 16, Ivan Kovac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 17, Dragica Tuskan?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 18, son Tuskan?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 19, Markobasic, Z?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 20, Baumgertner?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 21, Kuhar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 22, Dado Djukic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 23, Nikica Holjevac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 24, Damir Polhert?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 25, Zeljko Begov?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 26, Damjan Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 27, Gaspar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 28 and number 29, Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 30, Tomica Bajdrauh?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't put his name down, but we grew up together, we went to school together, so I didn't need to write his name down.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you about these two names that you've added here in the courtroom. They are not on this list. First of all, Tomislav Pap?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And the secondly, Jovanovic. And the name I don't know --

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oliver.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Oliver Jovanovic, was he on the list?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berghofer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then there was Pero Simonic from Dalmatinska Street. He wasn't on the list originally because I couldn't remember his name at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me, please, on the basis of the list that we have on the screen here, can you tell me who of these people were members of the defenders of Vukovar and the National Guard?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gavric was a haulier, and as to whether he later on worked at the hospital or not, I can't tell you, but I found him at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm only interested to find out who was in the guard or who were the defenders.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. Do you know what I can tell you, Mr. Vasic, the National Guards Corps was a formation, an armed uniformed formation. Maybe you should have asked me whether anyone had any uniforms, because if they had been members of the National Guards Corps, supposedly somebody would have provided them with uniforms and weapons. I suppose that would be a more logical way of putting the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, we have heard here that there are several categories of defenders of Vukovar, some were within the National Guards Corps, others were in other units of defence, and some were in the 204th Vukovar Brigade, et cetera. So what I'm asking you is: Do you know whether any of these people actively participated in the armed conflict on the Croatian side. Can we put it that way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about Sinisa Veber on the first -- on the first part of the list, no, perhaps the Kolak brothers, but I haven't seen them do anything. I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If you don't know, just tell us you don't know.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not, Mr. Vasic. I do not know for the simple reason that I never saw them on any positions. I never went to any positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Can you tell me whether you saw bandages on any of these people or plaster-casts or anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that number 22, Dado Djukic, he had a wound on his leg and he was walking on crutches.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And you never saw any -- anything like that in any of the others?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have only two questions left, and they have to do with the time when you returned to Croatia from Mitrovica. You were exchanged - isn't that right, Mr. Berghofer - in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know who you were exchanged with and who took you to this exchange operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berghofer. I'm only asking you to give me the information that you do know. Thank you very much indeed for providing me with the answers to my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no more questions left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, I'm Borivoje Borovic, the Defence counsel for Miroslav Radic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The first question for the witness: Since you talked about the ZNGs, and you gave us a somewhat detailed account of all that, what I'm interested in is the automatic rifles they had that you've already told us about. Where were they manufactured?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I never said anything about automatic rifles. I finished my military service back in 1961, and I was an artillery man.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just so as to -- not to waste any time, did you see any weapons in the hands of ZNGs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the ZNGs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time you're telling us this.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody has asked me about it before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And who did you lead in the breakthrough out of Vukovar when you were leading the column?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone to the last man were civilians, and I told you there were about 350 people. I couldn't remember the names of all of them, and I didn't know where they had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And why did the civilians go for the breakthrough? Why didn't they go to the hospital, just as you did?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many of these civilians, and I mean I -- it probably doesn't mean anything to you because as civilians -- even as civilians they did not survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, you're going to have to slow down a little. The interpreter is already breathless. A pause between --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What was your participation in this war? Did you have any military duties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, Mr. Borovic. I never had any military duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And after the war, did you get any financial compensation for the participation in war operations in Vukovar and did it become a part of your pension plan or retirement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean some kind of disability? Did I get some money?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you -- did it count as your time in the army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you reveal the secret as to how come you were considered to have participated in war and you have not participated in any combat operations, as you've just told us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Your Honours, do I need to answer this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, you do, I'm afraid. One significant question is whether you were a member of the Croatian forces or assisted in the defence of Vukovar. You've told us you were not, but you also tell us that the time you spent there has counted towards your military service. Those two appear inconsistent, so Mr. Borovic is asking you: Is there an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, Mr. Borovic, I'm going to try and explain this to you. I've stressed that I wasn't a member of the ZNGs, but we were recognised as defenders of Vukovar anyway and I'm proud of that. And I stress that I was in charge of food supplies, logistics, so that was my role.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see any of the defenders of Vukovar, as you call them, bearing arms?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On occasion they would come to the headquarters. Sometimes they would take the wounded away, sometimes they would come to my shop to visit my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That's another question. Thank you. Where was that headquarters that they visited and where you saw them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the headquarters that we organised, and I've told this to your colleague already, actually. We set it up in the Stjepan Radic street where there was the so-called Hungarian school in the past. Now it's the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they come armed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you be so kind as to tell us what sorts of weapons they had at the time when you used to see them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Russian automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that the members of the armed formations of Croatia had Russian automatic rifles? That was my first question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but back then we were not considered as the ZNGs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when did you start being considered as ZNGs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're now a Croatian state, acknowledged all our suffering after gaining independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in your opinion when did Croatia become independent? In what year?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that Croatia was occupied?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you in what year did it gain independence.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was still in Mitrovica, sir, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was it in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts. I do remember that all of our golden chains and anything that we had in gold was taken away from us in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether this entered the transcript. You said that it was indeed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less in the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I object to that. [Previous translation continues] ... the first time. What this witness's perception is what is independence or what is not is irrelevant to the issue. It may well become a legal issue in any event, but it's -- the perception of a person can often be different from the reality. That's irrelevant to issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, the question is asked of an ordinary lay witness. The ordinary lay witness has given an ordinary lay answer. It is not going to determine the question of law for this Chamber, should it become an issue in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you can relax.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, notwithstanding whether Croatia was recognised or not, you saw armed men. Apart from automatic rifles from Russia, did they have any other weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And they didn't even have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And did they have uniforms at a later stage, because you've said the ZNGs existed because you've already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have been recognised as being within the ZNGs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: No, thank you. What I want to ask is whether at any point before going to Mitrovica, did you see a live member of the ZNGs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe around the 15th of August, 1991, there were lots of soldiers in Vukovar, and there was a lot of joy and there was shooting in the air. There were pleased because they were leaving Vukovar. And I saw them in front of my shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But would you still answer my question, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's when I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The ZNGs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were wearing Croatian army uniforms. As to what formation they belonged to, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the right answer to my question. My question is the following: Could you describe the uniforms, the Croatian uniforms, or, rather, the ZNG uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were a kind of greenish colour. You know what colour it is. Perhaps slightly lighter than the ones worn by Mr. Sljivancanin back then, but I don't know really.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. What insignia did they have on their uniforms? Since you were a member of the military, you must know.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of the military, sir, and I didn't see what sort of insignia they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Since you had done your military service.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I was familiar with the insignia of the former Yugoslavia. I was familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was the commander-in-chief of the Croatian forces in Vukovar before you went to Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what day it was, but the fighting was well underway already and the shelling was getting heavy. Mile Dedakovic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that he was the commander-in-chief of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of Vukovar's defence. I'm not sure if he was ZNG or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever heard of Branko Borkovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed I have, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What was he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was Dedakovic's deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were these people previously military officers of the JNA, before they became commanders of the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know now because I'm -- I saw this on TV later on, that they had been in the JNA previously. But at the time I knew nothing about their background.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What exactly did you hear about them? Were they JNA officers? Which ranks did they have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. Back in 1997 and 1998, there were things being said on TV about them, but I can't remember specifically what.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But they were officers, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ranked officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Why did members of the ZNG display so much joy and why was there so much celebratory fire in August 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of those days. They were saying: There'll be a truce soon, there'll be a truce, no more war. The children were back from their summer holiday on the coast. I can't give you the exact date; don't hold me to it. And they were on their way out of the Danube Hotel. There was a lot of joy, and those uniformed young men were leaving Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the ZNG men when you talk about young uniformed men?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What on earth were they doing in the Danube Hotel in August 1991? What was there? Why were they there in the first place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I said, they probably heard that there would be no war; they believed it. And they were on their way back to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly that as early as August 1991 there were well-established military units, armed, uniformed, that were referred to as -- at the time, as the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in late August, but don't hold me to it. They all wore uniforms and they left Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where did they go? Just a minute, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there's something that we need to clear up. Page 21, line 19. I asked him about the Croatian forces, and he said August, but apparently the witness also said July. So the witness -- perhaps the witness can repeat this for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian forces, when were they set up, which month?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when they were set up. All I know is I saw them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was that July and August. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thereabouts. Maybe late July, early August. Thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since this question has now come along, what are armed Croatian units doing at the Danube Hotel in late July and early August? Were they perhaps stationed in that hotel? Was that a military facility, therefore?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But do you allow for the possibility that a military unit was stationed there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were eating there, they were sleeping there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Your neighbours, the people you tell us about, were most of them not people who fought alongside you in the defence of Vukovar? Were these people who had all served their regular military terms with the JNA, just like you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that not mean that both you and they had at some point in the JNA been trained to use weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a long time ago, in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: A -- an ex-JNA officer was at the head of those armed units and his deputy was also an ex-JNA officer. Do you agree that he would have been in a position to exercise command over people who were, regardless of their status, at some point trained to use weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that at least is my reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did the Croatian forces have a prison? You said something about that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember speaking about that, or at least I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'll try not to confuse you, and I'll try not to ask too much. You said yesterday: On our way we passed something that appeared to be a prison. Didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was in the former Yugoslavia when bikes were stolen, and this was some sort of a shed or a lost-and-found place where bikes were brought back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about the Croatian forces; more specifically, the ZNG forces that you saw back in July, did they have a flag of their own?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that. I only saw three or four cars drive by, shooting in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You led about 300 or 350 people on the breakthrough. You said you had an automatic rifle which you had previously traded or a gun. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you were heading a column comprising about 350 people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How do you know whether the remaining people in that column were armed or not, or perhaps you do not know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You also said that your group was preceded by another group?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How big was that group, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about 30 people in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And who put you in charge of leading that column of people on the breakthrough from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody put me in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you were self-appointed, in a way, and decided off your own bat to lead that column?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some people came over from the surrounding countryside. There were lots of people there. It was a long column and somebody had to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who organised for the people to assemble there or who organised the meeting where it was decided that you would attempt the breakthrough?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Josip Tomasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he have any military involvement in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a layman, like all of us, but he was much younger than I was. He was half my age.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But that's not what I asked. Did he have any military involvement? The fact that he was half as old as you makes no difference at all.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I said, he was not a professional. He just decided to join us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind and try to provide a more accurate description, since I seem to understand that you know something about his involvement.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This person lived at Lipovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And what was his involvement about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local Serbs at Lipovaca wanted to arrest him. It was for this reason that he hid in the boot of a car, and I don't know who eventually got him out of Vukovar or the other place, whatever its name was, Lipovaca. It so happened that I never saw him or met him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Still, that is not an answer to my question. I understand the -- about him hiding in the boot, but what about his later involvement? What exactly did he do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told Mr. Vasic previously, he was the commander of Vuka 1, Vuka 2, Vuka 3, which at one point became Osa 1, Osa 2, Osa 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What are all these things, Vuka and Osa?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some sort of check-points, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where was Osa 1 check-point?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drew it for you right there on that map yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just tell us.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Slavija area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about Osa 2?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some place in Patkoviceva Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about Osa 3?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some place between the Slavija area, Patkoviceva Street and the Dalmatinska area. It was somewhere in that area, among the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the so-called Danube Platoon of the Croatian forces stationed between the Eltz palace and the railway station? Have you ever heard of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Ivica Vujkovic is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know. He is five years younger than I, and we spent some time together when we were still children.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was he the commander of one of the platoons there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know for a fact that he was the commander of the Danube Platoon?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- well, since you claim to be familiar with the area, you've moved around Vukovar quite a lot, that at the Danube Hotel there were special forces from Bosanski Brod and from Opatovac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about the ZNG members who were firing in the air in late July and early August outside the Danube Hotel? Who did they belong to? Perhaps they were the very people I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were those people you recognised as locals or were they outsiders, someone who came from far away?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If those people had been people from Vukovar, I would have told you so immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you at one point in time all receive yellow Borovo boots, or rather, the factory's name was Polo? This was something that was produced for the American market. If so, at which point in time exactly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not given those, but I know that a handful of people did have those, about five people, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you at any point in time hear anything about the ZNG members all wearing the same kind of boots and they signed for these as early as February 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the Opatovac farm is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a very foggy idea. I drove through Opatovaci on my way to Novi Sad a hundred times or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of a person by the name of Ante Roso?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I remember. The name's not familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In your previous statements to the OTP and your testimony at the Belgrade Ovcara trial, you mentioned this so I must ask you about it. Before you went to Sremska Mitrovica, did you know the most important positions held by the ZNG inside Vukovar itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance now. I would like to show the witness these statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I've highlighted everything for you. The 26th of October, 2004, please, if you can find the 26th of October. Perhaps the best thing is to go straight to page 6. Page 6.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In English this is page 6, line 38. I'm not sure if you've got the right page, but can you please just read this aloud, the question by Attorney Perkovic, and then on from there, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next question, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next question is: Question --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Slowly. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next question is: "I fail to understand the witness. Was he a member of the 204th Brigade or not?"

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Everything that I've highlighted in yellow, please, read it out.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the 204th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My apologies. Could you please just also specify who is asking the question and who is providing the answer. There is the attorney and there is the witness. And you are the witness, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you didn't ask that of me originally, and I can now go back and read everything that I've read already.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Attorney Miroslav Perkovic: "My next question. I fail to understand the witness. Was he a member of the 2004th [as interpreted] Brigade or not?"

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So what is the witness's answer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Answer -- well, it continues here. Witness Victim Dragutin Berghofer: "Yes, I was a member." Attorney Perkovic: "Was Mr. Cakalic also a member of that brigade?" Witness Victim Dragutin Berghofer: "Well, you see, the 204th Brigade was holding Mitnica, Sajmiste, the hospital, Borovo, Priljevo, you see -- you see what I'm saying. All of us suddenly became the 204th Brigade. Okay. But that was after the war, the 204th Brigade, that was -- that it was recognised" --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, it doesn't say "recognised."

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "And when? Okay. It was after the war. There you go, the 204th, they called it the 204th."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: It says "they called it or recognised" -- it doesn't say "recognised it."

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They say they called it -- it says they called it the 204th Brigade. Is that all right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The 204th Vinkovci, and, well, there you go, Vukovarska 2, it was in fact -- but, it was the 2nd Company of the 1st Battalion. This -- that -- but Vukovar had not fallen yet. Let's say this was sometime in mid-October."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Berghofer, the question by the attorney is stated here. You answered you were a member of the 204th Brigade. You only found out it was called that after the war, just to be completely fair to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to the way this question is being put because it is misrepresenting what this witness is saying and his participation. My learned friend is slanting the question to suggest that he's involved in some military way. My learned friend is perfectly aware, that is the page that refers to the purchase of an airplane, and also the answer before he asks the question is reference to this witness being involved in a soup kitchen and feeding civilians, too. If he's going to try and read out a part to demonstrate military activity, he's got to read out the answers in toto to give the court a fair -- or to give the Court a proper context of what's being said. It's not a case for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, in these proceedings in 2004, you appear at one point to have accepted that you were a member of the 204th Brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I accepted him now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When did you become a member of the 204th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At some point after the 15th of September, 1991, and as far as I know, Your Honour, it didn't bear that name back then. I wasn't aware of it. It was much later that they said it was called the 204th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What was it that you became aware of that you became a member of? You said you didn't know it was the 204th Brigade but you became a member of something sometime after September. What did you become a member of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Zlatko Menges came along from [as interpreted] Mile Dedakovic, as far as I can remember, Your Honour, and he said: Guys, we're the 2nd Company of the 1st Battalion. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And was that of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Had we been the ZNGs, presumably we would have been assisted. We would have received some kind of help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us what the 2nd Company of the 1st Battalion was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was this group of people. There were some 70 or 80 of us, and we were manning Osa 1, 2, and 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you were a member of that group of 70 or 80 people, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was a cook and a warehouse keeper and I did a bit of logistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that was a group that was occupying three positions, Osa 1, 2, and 3. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that was sometime after late September of 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe it was perhaps already the beginning of October, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And what -- when did you first join that group of people, that 70 or 80 people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I had joined the others even earlier because I had no possibility of going anywhere or anything, but I was still guarding my shop. And on a daily basis we were still being told that there would be a truce, that there would be no war, and the radio and the TV or telling us that there will be no war, and so on. And had I known that there would be war, I would never ever have stayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And when did you first join this group of 70 or 80 people? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At some point in September, the beginning of September maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, your role in this group, you said you were doing some cooking and looking after supplies and some logistics. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What were other members of the group doing, the other people, this 70 or 80?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One drove a van. And -- you mean the 70 people there? Oh, yeah, they were up there at the Bojnice line, at Osa 1, 2, 3. It was the front line basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So they were manning positions, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And can you tell us whether they had weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some of them had automatic rifles, and some of them had hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I gather from what you've said, none of them had uniforms. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And did you continue to help as a member of this group until the 17th of November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, that may have cleared a few things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to ask you to put the evidence number 156 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You have to look at the screen.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Wait for it to appear.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, you know what I'm looking for. I don't see that it's the same document as the one in Belgrade, because there's no reference to the operation where I bought an ox, and you say that we bought a plane and it was an ox. I mean, this is a necessary correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: We did not talk about any planes. I am entitled to select the part of the transcript that I prefer, and if my learned friend wants to ask you about oxen and about planes, that's his problem, and it's not up to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please see Exhibit 156. We can see it now. Could you please blow up the middle of the picture a little bit. A little bit more, please. Still more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Since you've just confirmed, Mr. Berghofer, that you made a statement and you have the transcripts in front of you and you've read out the contents of your statement, I'm not going to start talking about your role, whether you were a member of the ZNG or another formation. But you, as a witness, made the following statement: "This Brigade, 204th, took Mitnica, Sajmiste, Bojnice, Priljevo, Borovo," and so on and so forth. Now, perhaps with the assistance of the usher you could mark these areas that you referred to on the map. Could you show us what area exactly was taken by the members of the 204th Brigade in the way in which you told us in the course of your testimony, Mitica [phoen].

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'll have to help me out. This arrow, as far as I can see, indicates the barracks. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is the barracks, the hospital, Nova Ulica, and Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to lead me through that. What do you want me to do? To indicate where -- members or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Since I'm not a member of the OTP, I'm not going to lead you. I'm not going to tell you what to show me. But I'm asking you: Since you had been in the army, you did your military service, you are familiar with the streets of Vukovar, could you just indicate by a line the area taken by the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know those lines. I know my zone and Slavija, where our lads were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just hang on a second. So you're not in a position to indicate what you've told us about as a witness in your witness statement, where exactly positions of the Croatian forces were when they took Mitica, Sajmiste, Bojnice, Borovo, and so on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can I do that? I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Thank you. The next question. Yesterday you mentioned the cellars - and do correct me if I'm wrong - but I believe you said that there were cellars, and then there were hills behind those cellars up to the height of 20 metres. Does it mean that those cellars were 20 metres below the ground?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There was some shelters in those cellars. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it possible for 2 or 300 people to fit into any of those shelters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was there a single shelter that could hold up to a thousand people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear about nuclear shelters and did you know where they were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of them, but it was somewhere in Olajnica, as we used to call that part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear about them existing at the hospital and Borovo Komerc?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but about some kind of Komerc, Borovo or something, but it was called "Komerc," that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And Vupik cellars, did they have any shelters that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had never been there, but even when I was a child I knew that those cellars were huge. Those were wine cellars, and I had heard of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What you read out earlier and what you heard about but you're unable to indicate on the map, well, in relation to that, my question is the following: Does this mean that if the 204th Brigade took Vitica [as interpreted], Sajmiste, the hospital, Borovo, Priljevo, does this mean that they had that part of town in their hands?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really understand your question. But Borovo, for example, would be used in order to prevent them from crossing the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about Vitica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For them not to come from the area of Sotin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean nobody was allowed to move freely, there were military front lines there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about Priljevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Priljevo was free. I only had heard about Borovo, but I didn't hear anything about Priljevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could walk freely. As far as I know, nobody was there, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But earlier on when you read out your witness statement, you confirmed that the 204th ZNG Brigade had taken the entire area, and you mentioned them taking Priljevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Priljevo is a part of Borovo as well, that is together, after Novi Most, after the new bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. When you said they took these areas, the ones that we've just listed, does this mean -- I mean, I'm not going to repeat all these names. What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was your language "they took." All I said was that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That's what you said, actually. You said that they had taken all these areas.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you must insist on that word, it's the same meaning, either they were there or they took it. It doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You also said to us that you heard over the loud-speaker that people were to go to the hospital. Is that right? You said that you heard that being said over the loud-speakers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll come back to that later. Okay. Let's move on. In answer to the question by my colleague Mr. Vasic as to whether Vesna Bosanac was ordering soldiers who had come to the hospital to discard their weapons and to change into civilian clothes, whether they were the ZNGs, you only gave a partial answer. Just as -- just in order to avoid any misunderstandings, can you please read the transcript from the Belgrade trial dated the 25th of October, 2004, page 68, and in the English version, page 64, lines between 9 and 10. It starts with the word "look." Could you please read it out to us. Page 68.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I start?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the right corner there is a reference to Vesna Bosanac. And then the witness Dragutin Berghofer: "Look, in those days we were running around, and then she said: There were -- yes. She said: There were lads who had uniforms, and I had an automatic rifle as well. And he says: Drop it" -- well, there seems to be something wrong with the text, but whatever, we'll try to make it sound okay. I can perhaps tell you from my memory. Apparently it says: "Drop your weapons and get changed. And I didn't have a uniform but I think" -- it says "October." "But I October -- it wasn't my" -- I don't know. There is a piece of the text missing. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please stop?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can see that the translation is very disorderly, and I am trying to read it now. And if I'm wrong, then the witness can perhaps tell me. So it is about the answer to the question as to whether Vesna Bosanac made a suggestion that they should change into civilian clothes, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. The witness said the following: "Look, we were just sitting around there for those two days, and then she said: There were lads in uniforms, and I myself had an automatic rifle, and then we said: Leave that, get changed, drop your weapons, and get changed. And I didn't have a uniform, and I don't think" - and it says "October," but it probably means automatic rifle - "was not mine, I don't know who I got it from, and I left it at the hospital next to a shed under a car, and as far as I know, it was not even in a working order." Is that right? Did I read it right properly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did, but some things are missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Whatever is missing, can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Quite simply, I came back --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: No. What I'm asking you about is it correct that you made this statement at the Belgrade trial at the Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know better what I said than you do, and I just wanted to complement this missing part of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got the automatic rifle. Just before we entered the woods, I exchanged it for a gun, and I didn't go for the breakthrough, and I came back to the hospital. There's five and six of us, and I've said it before. And then I hid the automatic rifle straight away next to the shed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Does that mean that you came to the hospital carrying on automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Why did you hide the automatic rifle near the shed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't had it for three and a half months and now I was back in town and what use did I have for it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So why did you take it all the way back from the woods to the hospital if you had no use for it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't think I would have discarded it just because of those 600 metres there, right? I just hid it under a burnt-out car next to a shed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honours, but I believe this is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You seem to be at a point where it was not practical to stop you, but clearly now we've reached that point. We must now adjourn for a time to allow the tapes to be rewound and to give the witness a little break. We will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, when you were in the hospital on the 19th of November, I think you said that you saw Kuzmic there, right, with two young soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe what Kuzmic was wearing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wearing a JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was there a rank displayed on the uniform?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I got a sideways look of him and I didn't see the rank. But let me tell you straight off, I didn't see a single rank anywhere that I can remember on any of those men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You've testified yesterday that there was a combat vehicle at the head of the column, which you referred to as a Campagnola. To be perfectly precise, this was on page 5287, lines 8 through 13. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: We heard that you did your regular military term with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: There are two different sorts of combat vehicles. One is a tank with a caterpillar, and the other is a transport vehicle with regular tires, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have the following document displayed on the screen, please. This is document 0467-5486. Can we please zoom in a little? If we can't, that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: We mentioned one combat vehicle as being a tank with a caterpillar, and the other was a transport vehicle. Was it this sort of vehicle?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: There is a transcript from the Ovcara case, you should have it in front of you. Could you please go to the 25th of October, 2004. The B/C/S reference is page 72. And for the benefit of my learned friend Mr. Moore, the English reference is page 67, line 26. You can follow and I will read. I can see that you're having a hard time reading, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I was having a hard time, but it wasn't consistent what I was looking at. But you can just go ahead and read.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You follow what I'm saying, and if I make any mistakes please say so. So I'm reading the relevant portion from page 72 of the transcript. Attorney Todorovic's question: "Were they going in a column?"

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please don't answer, just listen. The witness's answer:" Yes. " Counsel Todorovic: "Were these being secured by military vehicles?" "Answer: "They were just there, they were on the bus, a young soldier was." Counsel Todorovic: "My question is: Was the column being secured?" Answer: "No. And since I was on the fourth bus, I didn't see ahead of us or what was going on behind us. But there was a young soldier on the bus." Is this true what you stated at the Belgrade trial?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: Is it true you were on the fourth bus?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I remember it, yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And when the column was on its way, you couldn't see what was ahead of you at the head of the column, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's only when there was a bend in the road that I was able to see a military Campagnola vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said: "A combat vehicle that I call Campagnola."

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military vehicle, military vehicle. Because Campagnola is a military vehicle and not a combat vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But now you've just confirmed this. Counsel Todorovic asked you a crystal clear question and your answer was that nobody was providing security for this column, nor, you say, were you able to see any bends. If I tell you that yesterday was your first reference ever to this Campagnola and you have provided a large number of different statements, did perhaps someone talk you into mentioning this Campagnola vehicle right here, right now, for the first time? If so, who was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't just make it up, but I don't know where you get this information from, that I never referred to it. But at the Belgrade trial -- I'm not really that clever. I can't keep so many different things in my head all at once.
